title: Stellar Endings: Supernovae and Black Holes

cues.text: Massive stars end when their core turns to iron, which consumes energy instead of releasing it.
With no outward pressure left, gravity causes a sudden, catastrophic collapse.
The infalling material bounces off the dense core,
sending a powerful shockwave that blasts the star's outer layers into space.
In binary systems, a white dwarf can steal gas from a neighbor,
slowly gaining mass until it hits the Chandrasekhar limit.
Once that limit is reached, the pressure triggers a runaway nuclear reaction,
causing the entire star to detonate as a Type Ia supernova.
After a massive star explodes, a dense core remnant is left behind. If this core is heavy enough, it cannot stabilize.
Gravity crushes this core into a singularity,
a point of infinite density where all the star's mass is packed into almost no space.
The event horizon forms around this point,
creating a boundary of no return where gravity is so strong that even light cannot escape.
Both supernova types and black hole formation are triggered by the star running out of nuclear fuel.
A supernova is the violent expulsion of a star's outer layers, driven by either core collapse or runaway fusion.
A black hole forms only when the remaining core is so massive that gravity crushes it completely,
